newsitem.title: USA: Conoco, PDVSA seek arranger for $1.3 bln loan.
newsitem.headline: Conoco, PDVSA seek arranger for $1.3 bln loan.

text.p: E.I. Dupont de Nemours & Co energy unit Conoco and state-owned Petroleos de Venezuela subsidiary Maraven have invited 23 banks to compete to arrange $1.3 billion in senior debt financing for their Petrozuata joint venture, sources said on Thursday.
The loan would represent the bulk of the debt portion of the oil development project, which has a total cost of $2.2 billion.

The partners are expected to name an arranger or arrangers for the commercial bank loan by the end of the first quarter and determine financing sources in the first half of 1997. All financing is scheduled to close by October, sources said.

The actual amount of the offering will depend on the credit rating, sources said. The partners have already held preliminary meetings with rating agencies Standard & Poor's, Moody's and Duff & Phelps and are aiming for an investment grade rating.

The Maraven-Conoco venture is the first of at least five proposed Venezuelan upgrading deals to reach the financing stage and its success in raising capital would pave the way for the other deals to move forward.
Other companies involved in proposed ventures include ARCO, Phillips, Texaco, Mobil, Exxon, Total, Norsk Hydro and Statoil.
Maraven and Conoco signed their joint venture on November 10, 1995. They plan to begin drilling this year to recover 1.5 billion to 2.0 billion of extra-heavy crude.
In 1998, the companies will begin building a delayed coker at the Venezuelan coastal city of Jose to convert the crude. The facility is due on line in 2000.
Petrozuata will first pump 65,000 bpd of oil around August 1998. Another 65,000 bpd will come on stream in late 1999 to coincide with the start-up of the coker.
At least part of the syncrude would be processed at Conoco's U.S. refineries, including its Lake Charles facility.

This week, Conoco announced that Petrozuata awarded four pipe supply contracts for the 125-mile, (200 kilometer) 36-inch pipeline that will transport the crude from the Zuata region of the tar belt to Jose.
The belt, known in Spanish as the Faja, contains an estimated 270 billion barrels of recoverable extra-heavy crude reserves.
